meaning: a bell-founder (an East-Anglian term)
author_comment: An East-Anglian term. No instances appear in the Hundred Rolls (1273). 'Belleʒetare (bellyatere), campanarius': Prompt. Parv. In the Register of Wills (London), ii. 226, occurs 'William Burford, billeytere.' I forgot to look for the date of this. Stowe informs us that Billiter Lane was once known as Belʒeters Lane. This settles the origin of the surname. 'In 1349, Thomas de Baldeswell presented to the Church aforesaid as chief lord of this fee: in 1367, Adam Humphrey: and in 1385, Adam Pyk, and in 1400, Edmund Belytter, alias Belzeter' (Blomefield's Norfolk, viii. 383).
notes: Cited in the author's commentary. Presented to the Church as chief lord of the fee in 1400. Also called Edmund Belzeter
source: History of Norfolk (Blomefield and Parkin), vol. viii, p. 383

meaning: the son of Bell; v. Bell (1)
author_comment: There is no evidence in favour of 'the son of Bill,' i.e. William. That nick. is comparatively modern. In the Modern Domesday Book (co. Warwick) there are four Bellisons, one Belson, and one Bilson, all evidently of the same stock, namely, Bellson (i.e. the son of Isabella). Bilson is an easy variant of Belson.
source: Allegations for Marriage Licences issued by the Bishop of London, 1520-1828 (Harleian Society), i. 21
record_text: 1561. Thomas Bilson and Margery Pussye: Marriage Lic. (London), i. 21.
